summary:
Five steps. The third one found a defect in the second-to-last turn's work.

**A screen model.** ScreenBuffer is a small VT interpreter â€” cursor movement, erasure, text, nothing
else. Readiness now matches the rendered screen anchored to the last drawn line, because the earlier
measurement showed an agent's last bytes are wherever the cursor went rather than what the user sees.
The built-in markers are anchored at both ends and remain explicitly unverified against a ready agent.

**The trust gate is a state.** NeedsAttention, searched across the whole screen, outranking readiness,
announced once per transition rather than per repaint. Before this the shell refused and said nothing,
which is indistinguishable from a broken pane (DC-011).

**The joins, on a real repository â€” and DC-022.** The first run over TheTerrace reported 7,426
verified joins, each carrying "declared in the resource's dependsOn", in a repository containing no
Bicep and no dependsOn at all. depends_on is the C# extractor's predicate for type dependencies; the
join qualified on the PREDICATE rather than the kind of thing it was on, and its basis was a fixed
string that could never disagree with the evidence. It failed in the flattering direction â€” the
largest Verified count the pane had ever shown. Fixed, pinned by two tests, registered. After the fix:
0 verified, 59 inferred, which is the correct answer for that repository.

The contexts pane in the same run is usable, and names Operations as the boundary worth examining.
360 of 474 uncovered symbols are tests â€” the namespace grouping turned a number that reads as a gap
into a line that reads as correct.

**Two controls widened.** The fixture-derivation gate now watches command ids (29 identifiers,
observed firing on a planted literal), and the migration chain has both an end-to-end test and one
asserting the steps join up â€” which fails the moment a version is bumped without a migration.

Reported: "the agent sessions do not have my profile or my environment variables â€” ghcp and claude
are both installed so they should both work."

The verified cause is not in this product. The machine's PATH is 22,297 characters and cmd.exe
silently drops a variable that large, so every .cmd shim â€” which is every npm-installed CLI â€” starts
with an EMPTY PATH and cannot find node, git or itself. claude works because claude.exe is a real
executable with no cmd in the path; ghcp does not exist at all, and the Copilot CLI has an npm .cmd
shim. That asymmetry is the entire symptom.

Necessary and sufficient, both measured: at 22,297 characters a cmd child receives an empty PATH,
reproduced twice including once with no part of AI-DE involved; trimmed to 1,799 characters the same
child receives the full PATH. AI-DE passes the environment correctly â€” PowerShell started from the
same inherited block reads all 22,297 characters and resolves claude.

Five hypotheses were ruled out with evidence, including one flag removed and re-measured, and the
belief that the profile was at fault â€” which is where two turns of work went first, because the
symptom is indistinguishable from a launcher bug.

The cause of the 22,297 characters: roughly 190 entries of the shape Temp\biohacker-nuget-<guid>\
dotnet-home\.dotnet\tools, appended to the PERSISTED user PATH by another project's build tooling and
never removed. Each is unique, so there is nothing to de-duplicate.

nothing saying why. EnvironmentHealth.Inspect now states the size, the limit and the largest repeated
group â€” because 200 unique paths is a number, not a lead â€” announced once per shell, never per pane.
It does not edit PATH: a tool that silently rewrites the environment to make itself work has hidden
the problem from the only person who can fix it.

half of the request and makes .ps1 shims resolve. It is recorded honestly as NOT fixing the reported

summary:
A second language, and a paging defect the second language exposed.

PythonExtractor reads modules, top-level classes and functions, and import edges. Six repositories
had disclosed unread Python before it existed; the disclosure was right and it is not a substitute,
because a graph that says "there is Python here and I cannot see it" is honest and still blind.

It reads STRUCTURE, not semantics, and says so on every scope: imports are not resolved, nested
declarations are invisible, dynamic imports are not followed. Declarations are recognised at column

symbol in the graph that no importer can reach. Import edges are INFERRED, because the target is the
module path as written and whether it resolves to anything is not established here; calling that
Verified is precisely the defect DC-022 is about. A simplify: marker records the ceiling and the
upgrade trigger.

(subject, predicate, object) is NOT unique â€” two scopes can assert the same triple â€” so a cursor over

summary:
The extraction profile is explained, and both earlier conclusions were artefacts of the benchmark.

A fresh .NET process reading 120 newly-created files took 493ms (4.11ms/file); a SECOND fresh process
over the same files took 6ms, and the repository's own source reads at 0.19ms/file. So the ~500ms
was a one-time, system-wide, per-file cost on the first read after creation â€” the signature of
on-access scanning â€” and it never recurs. It is not extraction's cost at all.

Run against a real repository the profile inverts completely. TheTerrace, 463 files in its main
scope: read 53ms, parse 694ms, walk 1,167ms. The walk is the LARGEST cost on real code and looked
free on the synthetic workload, because the generated types were trivial â€” no inheritance, no
generics, four fields each.

Two independent flaws in one generator, each inverting a published conclusion. Registered as DC-028:
a synthetic benchmark measures the benchmark unless its workload resembles the real one in the
dimensions that drive cost. The control is that the spike prints the same timings for named real
repositories, so the synthetic figure and the real one appear side by side.

Python imports are resolved within their scope now. An import naming a module the scope contains
points at a file that exists and was read, so the edge is VERIFIED; anything else stays INFERRED with
the name as written, because it may be a package, a module in another scope, or nothing, and
asserting which is the guess DC-022 is about. Relative imports resolve against the importing module's
package, one level per leading dot, and climbing above the root resolves to nothing rather than
throwing. On the real Python repository 82 of 330 imports now resolve, and the disclosure carries the
count of those that do not â€” a blanket "imports are not resolved" became a closed gap reported as
open the moment resolution landed.

The cursor audit found one more thing and cleared another. ResultBounds.NextCursor is ALWAYS null and
no projection returning it pages â€” said out loud in the type, because a caller could loop on it and
never leave the first page with nothing failing. And DeriveClaimCurrent folds statuses with Max under
a comment saying the weakest wins: correct only because the enum is ordered strongest-first, so a
reordering would silently invert it into manufacturing confidence. Pinned by a test.

summary:
The hypothesis that `ToDisplayString` dominated the symbol walk was **wrong**, and measuring it found
a much larger defect than the one it was looking for.

Splitting the walk by operation: display 46ms across 7,312 calls â€” **3.9%**. The real costs were
depends-on 613ms (51%) and attributes 403ms (34%). The attribute cost was one call:
`FluentTableMappings` ran `DescendantNodes()` over all 1,026 type declarations, hunting an EF
`ToTable` call. Hoisting it to the compilation with a source-text prefilter cut it to 1ms of
prefilter across 465 files and 217ms of walking the 66 that survived.

Then the 66 files were the finding. Most were EF migration `*.Designer.cs` snapshots â€” and the three
that were not revealed that the reader **did not work**. It matched `Entity<T>()...ToTable("x")` as a
single expression. TheTerrace, like most EF codebases, writes:

    var terrace = modelBuilder.Entity<Terrace>();
    terrace.ToTable("Terrace", "setup");

So the extractor recovered **1 declared mapping and guessed 123**, on a repository that states every
one of them outright. Every one of those 123 inferred `maps_to` edges was a name-matching guess
standing where a declaration already existed. The same reader also emitted the entity name as
written in source (`Order`) where every other assertion uses the display string (`Shop.Order`) â€” so
even its successes were edges whose subject matched no node.

Resolved semantically now: ask the model for the RECEIVER's type. One rule answers every style â€”
chained, local-variable, lambda-configuration, `IEntityTypeConfiguration<T>` â€” because in all of them
the receiver is an `EntityTypeBuilder<TEntity>`, and the symbol's display string is the name the rest
of the extractor emits. **Verified joins 1 â†’ 64, inferred 123 â†’ 73, `declares_table` facts 63.**

Generated files are skipped, on correctness grounds before performance ones: EF writes a model
snapshot per migration, each calling `ToTable` for every entity *as it stood then*, so reading them
asserts a table renamed three migrations ago as current fact wearing the same Verified badge. 63 of
the 66 files were these. `fluent-scan` fell 1,418ms â†’ 60ms warm as a side effect, not as the goal.
The skip is disclosed with a count, because skipped is not absent.

DC-032 registered: **a reader recognises one spelling of a pattern and reports the rest as absent.**
The signature is a ratio nobody looks at â€” precise hits against fallback hits on real input â€” and it
survives because the fallback is doing its job, so the surface looks populated and coverage stays
green. The control was observed failing with the skip disabled.

**Module ids were colliding, certainly rather than theoretically.** Both module-shaped extractors
named a module by its path relative to its OWN SCOPE, and a scope is one directory. Every Python
package has an `__init__.py`, so a repository with five packages produced five scopes each declaring
a module called `__init__` â€” one node in the graph carrying the merged edges of five unrelated files.
The same for `index.ts`, `main`, `setup`, `conftest`. Ids are now the repository-relative path:
unique by construction, readable, and the string a person would type to open the file.

summary:
**The measurement the sub-scope decision was blocked on now exists.** A refresh had a span but its
STATUS carried no duration, so the only thing a caller could read was how many assertions came back.
`ScopeRefreshStatus` now carries `QueuedMilliseconds` and `DurationMilliseconds` â€” kept separate
because waiting is a concurrency problem and running is a cost problem, and one number hides which
one a user is feeling. `RefreshMetrics` adds p50/p95/max over a bounded window plus first/last
observed, exposed over IPC as `refresh.metrics` with no request body and no failure mode: an operator
asking what re-indexing costs should never be told it depends on what they enable first.

Deliberately **no rate is computed**. "Refreshes per hour" from two samples is a number with no error
bar that gets quoted as if it had one; the raw facts let a reader compute it when there is enough of
it to mean something and notice when there is not. Failed refreshes are timed too â€” a run that takes
twenty seconds and then throws is the one an operator most wants to see, and excluding failures is
how a percentile ends up describing only the easy cases. With nothing measured everything reports
zero and null rather than an interpolation of nothing.

**No tracked project escapes compilation now.** `spikes/joins-on-a-real-repo` â€” the harness behind
nearly every performance and join number in this log â€” is not in `AiDe.sln`, so a change to

MEASURED: the whole-graph response is 1,522,284 bytes against a 1,048,576-byte IPC frame. It could

writing and returns a new `ipc.payload_too_large` carrying the actual and permitted byte counts.
Checked before rather than caught after on purpose: a partially written frame leaves the peer reading
a length prefix whose body never arrives, which is a hang rather than an error. The writer's own throw
is correct and stays.

summary:
The graph was found by a user opening a repository, not by us, so every other read operation was
measured at its own ceiling against the 1 MiB frame. **Two more were one repository away from
INV-0003, and a third could never have succeeded.**

| operation | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| evidence (2,000/page) | 1,004,397 B â€” **95.8% of the frame** | 659,164 B, 1,310 rows, cursor continues |
| graph (5,000-node ceiling) | 1,522,915 B â€” **overflows** | 474,437 B, shrunk to fit, `Omitted` reports |
| find (20,000 ceiling) | 461,750 B returned while **reporting a 64 KiB cap** | byte-bounded, `ByteCapped` set |

The class behind all three: **every ceiling in the read surface counts ITEMS and the transport limit
is in BYTES**, and every item's size comes from repository content. A count-only cap admits an
unbounded payload. `Evidence`'s own documentation claimed a page "can cross a pipe without breaching
the result-byte cap" â€” it was fifteen times over that cap. `Find` declared `MaxBytes: 65,536` beside
461,750 bytes of results, a control that could not fire (DC-016).

Truncating an evidence page is **lossless**, which is why the bound belongs in the projection: the
cursor continues from the last row actually returned, so it costs a round trip and never a row. A
test pages a corpus to exhaustion and asserts every assertion comes back exactly once. Every response
keeps at least one item â€” a caller that receives nothing because its first row is enormous can never
make progress.

The byte guard uses a **measured** constant, not a guessed one: 2,000 assertions whose fields total
238,002 bytes serialise to 1,004,397, so JSON scaffolding is **383 bytes per row**. Rounded up,
because a guard that under-counts is a guard that lets the frame overflow.

**The sub-scope-incrementality decision is resolved, and not by the instrument built for it.** The
note said the answer depended on how often edit-to-graph happens, and `RefreshMetrics` was built to
measure that. One grep answered it instead: **there is no `FileSystemWatcher` anywhere in `src/`**.
Indexing runs only from explicit commands, so the cost is paid deliberately by a user pressing a
button. Breaking the per-scope snapshot's atomicity to shorten a deliberate 1.2s action is a poor
trade, so none of options Aâ€“D is built. The note stays, status `resolved`, naming the trigger that
would change it: **re-index on save**, which converts a bounded cost into a per-edit one.

Worth recording because it nearly went the other way. Three hypotheses in this area have now been
wrong â€” `ToDisplayString` (3.9%), `SymbolEqualityComparer` (0.5%), "the index still walks every
scope" (it does not). This would have been the fourth: collecting a distribution and reasoning
carefully about a number that answered a question nobody was asking.

**My own new gate cried wolf and is fixed.** `verify-id-allocators` reported an undeclared family
called `nDC-` â€” it was matching the `n` of a JSON-escaped newline before a *mentioned* `DC-` id in a
log summary. A mention is not an allocation, which is the same distinction the first draft got wrong
when it read ADR ids out of `architecture.md`. Fixed with a lookbehind, and the narrative files are
excluded from the candidate scan: a record of a mention must never nominate an allocator. This is the
second time this script has flagged correct behaviour as a defect; a control that does that twice is
one people switch off.

drilling in draws. For every group, not a sampled one â€” the interesting failure is the group whose
naming rule differs, and that is never the group a test author picks by hand. Both paths compute
membership from one definition (`GraphOverview.GroupFor`), which is why the round trip holds.

**Proven across the pipe.** The overview is nested â€” clusters and weighted links â€” so it is the
response most likely to arrive with an inner list flattened or a count defaulted to zero, and a
cluster's count is a claim a user can check. The daemon test now drills from the largest cluster back
to its nodes and asserts the counts agree.

measurement in this project had come from TheTerrace. Running BioHacker (32 scopes, no `DbContext` at

because a column that no longer exists is a **wrong** fact rather than a missing one. Renames are
counted and disclosed rather than guessed: every dialect spells them differently, and guessing
produces a confidently wrong column name.

**Three gates I wrote this session were not in CI.** `verify-id-allocators`,
`verify-project-coverage` and `verify-bounds-are-enforced` sat in `tools/` for several commits with
no workflow line â€” they ran only when I remembered. A gate nobody invokes is the "lesson recorded as
prose" failure wearing an executable's clothes: it looks like a control in every review and fires
never. All three wired, and `verify-project-coverage` now asks the same question about gates that it
asks about projects â€” **what exists to be run, and is not run.** Observed failing with a gate removed
from the workflow.

**The `simplify:` marker audit found one triggered and one premise already false.** `IpcFraming`'s
trigger fired during INV-0003 â€” and the answer was **none of the two exits the marker listed**.
Neither a bigger frame nor a data lane: the operation did not legitimately need to carry more. A
2,815-node hairball was never a useful answer and the spec had always said so, so every response was
bounded below the cap instead. Recorded, because a marker naming two exits invites you to take one.

Its stated premise â€” *"a control lane carries envelopes, not payloads: the largest legitimate message
is a command with a small JSON body"* â€” was **already false when audited**: ordinary responses are an
evidence page at 659,164 bytes, a graph at 475,223, an overview at 345,507. That sentence had not
been re-read since it was true. The other twelve markers were reviewed with no evidence of firing.

better than the feature.** BioHacker has zero `DbContext` files, zero `[Table]` attributes and 191

against three tables is not *mapped* to any of them.

summary:
**I shipped a defect last turn and this turn's sweep caught it.** The `uses_table` reader matched a
SQL keyword followed by a word ANYWHERE in a string literal, so *"we update the record"* produced an
edge to a table called `the`. MEASURED: 63 prose strings in TheTerrace, and its `uses_table` count
fell from **150 to 56** once the reader required a statement SHAPE.

Under-matching hides real facts; over-matching invents them â€” and the invented ones are worse,
because they arrive labelled **Verified**. Same root cause as DC-033 in the opposite direction: the
matcher's fit to real input had never been measured. **A matcher is not finished until you know both
what it misses and what it invents.**

**The naive fix broke the real case, which is exactly why both directions must be measured
together.** Requiring each literal to begin with a verb found **nothing at all** on the repository
that motivated the feature â€” real code splits SQL across concatenated literals, and the fragment
holding `FROM dbo.AssessmentJob` begins with `FROM`. The reader folds the `+` chain and reads it as
one statement; a chain containing anything non-literal is skipped whole rather than half-read.

A smaller lesson: the regex form of that shape test silently returned false for
`"INSERT INTO dbo.AssessmentJob (â€¦)"` â€” a string plainly beginning with one of its own alternatives â€”
and cost more to diagnose than the check was worth. It is explicit code now.

**`uses_table` reaches the Joins pane.** A distinct kind, never folded into `maps_to`: a store class
issuing four statements against three tables is not mapped to any of them, and counting usage as
mapping would make the verified/inferred ratio the pane exists to show meaningless. BioHacker's pane
goes from **0 verified / 8 inferred to 57 / 8** â€” a repository that showed nothing now shows what its
code actually touches.

**Step 2 needed no work and step 3 was answered by measurement.** The EF reader ALREADY folds
`CreateTable`, `AddColumn`, `DropColumn`, `DropTable`, `RenameTable` and raw `Sql` â€” I assumed it
might not, without checking, which is the habit this session keeps catching. Measured against real
usage: the operations it does not handle (`CreateIndex` 113, `AddForeignKey` 19, `AlterColumn`) do
not change which tables or columns EXIST. One genuine gap found and closed: `RenameColumn` was
unhandled with no default case, so a renamed column silently kept its old name â€” a wrong fact. EF
states renames in named arguments, so unlike raw SQL it is simply readable.

**Python and TypeScript do not embed SQL, so nothing was built for them.** The counts looked
promising â€” 186, 61, 1,162 "SQL literals" â€” and sampling showed *"update the"*, *"select more than
one option from this"*, and **zero** files containing `insert into`. Building `uses_table` there
would have emitted edges from English prose. Evidence for NOT building something is worth as much as
evidence for building it.

**The measurement log earns its keep at two readings.** Verified joins across the three repositories
moved **64 â†’ 120**, **0 â†’ 57**, **35 â†’ 50**, with assertion counts slightly DOWN as prose noise left
the graph. One reading is a point; two is a direction, and the drift is now in `git diff` rather than
in my memory of last turn's numbers.

summary:
**The invent-direction of DC-033 now has a control, and it found four more defects on its first
run.** `ExtractorsDoNotInventTests` feeds every reader a corpus with no declarations and plenty of
text SHAPED like declarations, and asserts it produces nothing but disclosures:

- the **SQL** reader read `-- CREATE TABLE Ghost` and `/* CREATE TABLE Historical */` as tables;
- the **TypeScript** reader read `export class Removed {}` out of a block comment;
- the **Python** reader read a class out of a **docstring** â€” the one place its column-zero rule
  cannot tell documentation from declaration;
- the **C#** reader turned *"delete from your account to remove it"* into `table:your`, because that
  sentence genuinely begins with a SQL verb and last turn's shape test could not reject it.

**Commented-out code is the worst possible input for a line-oriented reader**, and every repository
is full of it â€” it is real syntax, because it *was* code. `SourceText` blanks comments before any
reader believes a line, keeping newlines so provenance line numbers stay true. The C# case needed a
second rule: a real table reference **ends where a clause can begin** â€” a keyword, punctuation, or
the end of the statement. In prose the next token is just another word.

**Two things the fixes got wrong first, kept because they are the lesson.** Blanking string contents
for SQL deleted `"main"."Thing"`: in SQL a double quote is a quoted IDENTIFIER, not a string, so the
reader lost the very names it exists to find â€” caught by a test in seconds, which is the cheapest
possible way to learn that two languages disagree about a quote character. And `PRINT 'about to
create table X'` names no table while `EXEC('CREATE TABLE â€¦')` does; the reader can tell neither from
the other, so it reads neither and discloses the count.

**Step 1 was answered by measurement and needed no change.** The Bicep and context readers were swept
on a repository they were not written against: Bicep's matchers are line-anchored on `resource`,
`module` and `param`, and their values came back as real parameter names (`sqlServerName`,
`identityName`) and real Azure types â€” nothing invented. The context map's `*` is a documented suffix
wildcard and the real patterns end at a `.` boundary. Both pinned by the new control so they stay
that way.

**The third reading shows the CORRECTION, which is what a third reading is for.** Verified joins:

    TheTerrace                64 -> 120 -> 95
    BioHacker                  0 ->  57 -> 55
    meridian-finance-planner  35 ->  50 -> 46

The middle number was inflated by prose; the last is the honest one. **A single reading would have
recorded 120 as progress**, and two readings would have recorded it as a trend.

**On `AlterColumn` â€” the decision, not an assumption.** It is not folded, and should not be. The
graph's `has_column` records that a column EXISTS; `AlterColumn` changes a type or nullability, which
that fact does not carry, so folding it would change nothing observable. Recording types is a
different feature â€” it would need a fact shape that can express them, both schema readers agreeing on
it, and a consumer that wants it. None of those exists, so this stays where it is: named in the
extractor's `simplify:` ceiling as the upgrade trigger, rather than half-built.

**The knowledge graph was never being populated, and the reason is worse than a bug.** The reader had
existed since Phase 1, with tests, inside the fixture extractor. `CompositeExtractor` had a route for
it. And `CSharpScopeDiscovery` produced six scope kinds â€” `csharp`, `bicep`, `schema`, `python`,
`typescript`, `sql` â€” and **no knowledge scope at all**. The capability was correct, tested, and
unreachable on every real repository for the life of the project.

Both halves passed their own tests. The producer is proven by unit tests that hand it input; the
router is proven by fixtures that name the scope explicitly. Only DISCOVERY was untested against
reality, and its gap is invisible from either side.

**A zero that means "nobody looked" reads as "there is none"** â€” which is the shape this product
exists to avoid, in the product's own headline surface, on a repository whose premise is that *docs
hold intent, code holds reality, and the expensive defects live in the gap*. Half of that sentence
was never being read.

MEASURED after wiring discovery, on this repository: **466 `owned_by`, 346 `refines`, 287
`implements`, 272 `relates-to`, 66 `depends-on`**, centred on `knowledge-hub` with 78 edges. Scopes
across the three measured repositories: **28â†’66, 34â†’48, 34â†’56**. Every response still fits the frame.

**Running it over real documents immediately found two defects in the new reader** â€” which is the
lesson from last turn applied one turn later:

- link lines carry a trailing YAML comment, and trimming from the END left it attached: the graph
  gained a relation literally called `implements }   # typed edges â€” registry in â€¦`. Parsing now
  stops at the closing brace.
- **templates** carry frontmatter in exactly the shape a real document does, with `<artifact-id>`
  where the id goes â€” so they became nodes describing the shape of a document, linked to things that
  do not exist. Excluded by filename and, independently, by rejecting angle-bracketed placeholders.

DC-041 registered: **a capability is complete, tested, and nothing ever routes work to it.** The
signature is a count that is exactly zero on every real repository while a sibling count is large,
and the question that finds it is *"what produces the keys this router matches on, and does it
produce this one?"*. The control compares the two lists in a test instead of in somebody's head:
`EveryRouteHasAProducerAndEveryProducerHasARoute` fails if discovery emits a kind nothing routes, or
if a route exists that nothing discovers.

**The other next steps, carried:**

- **Bicep is comment-stripped too.** It PASSED the invent control â€” line-anchored matchers, and a
  sweep of an unfamiliar repository produced only real parameter names and real Azure types. Stripped
  anyway: it was the last line-oriented reader still parsing raw text, and all three readers caught
  inventing were caught reading commented-out code.
- **Provenance line numbers are asserted, not assumed.** Comments are blanked rather than deleted
  precisely so a claim can still be opened at the right line; a test now pins `5:1` for a table
  declared after a multi-line comment. It was the reason for the design and had never been checked.
- **The invent control now runs against real repository text**, which is how both knowledge defects
  surfaced â€” synthetic noise is written by the same person as the reader (DC-028's shape).
- **`GraphQuery` filters: ANSWERED by the user â€” presets, three named views.** Recorded in the
  contract with the three query shapes (Domain / Everything / This project). `Kinds` is deliberately
  not one of them: it is a refinement *within* a view, and folding it in would rebuild the

resource and python module carried one, so almost the entire graph was classified `knowledge`, and it
surfaced exactly as the design session saw it: a bicep resource reading **"kind: knowledge"**. DC-022
precisely â€” a predicate gained producers and a consumer kept its assumption about who emits it.

**Fixed by having the PRODUCER declare it.** Scope-id prefixes were the first attempt and were nearly
right, but the fixture reader emits knowledge from a scope not named for it, so the id could not be
the authority either. A fact can be: both knowledge-reading paths now emit `node_class = knowledge`,
and the core classifies from that. Nothing infers a node's half of the graph from a type name again.

**Neighbours carry their real kind.** `DescribeResult` gained `NeighborKinds`; the canvas hardcoded

whose every row is an artefact of re-running the indexer cannot answer the question it exists for.

fixed list of type names cannot work across repositories, and widening the list only moves the

and code are not linkable and orthogonal, they will tend to be orthogonal which is why pruning the
graph on one or the other is a meaningful cut. Do not infer â€” the graph should only be on observable
links/relationships."*

Recorded as a decision note, because it is a standing principle rather than one answer: **an edge is
a claim that something in the repository says so.** Orthogonality is information â€” because the two
halves are separate, "show the knowledge" and "show the code" are exact cuts rather than blurred
ones. Inference would have made membership depend on how good the guess was that day, and this
codebase has paid for that twice already (`depends_on` produced 7,426 false Verified edges;
`uses_table` turned *"we update the record"* into a table called `the`). What would legitimately
unblock a join is a link written down â€” `- { to: TheTerrace.Features.Fixtures, rel: governs }` â€” which
the frontmatter reader would index today with no code change.

statically, so reading them would be inference â€” ruled out by the principle above. Nested
declarations are observable but MEASURED at 28/31/21 against 356/457/150 top-level across three

summary:
**The cap-before-filter sweep, run properly this time.** Every bounded read in the projection service
was checked rather than spot-sampled: `Find` filters inside `SearchNodeIds`, `Describe` inside
`AssertionsTouching`, `Impact` inside `OutgoingAssertions`, `Evidence` inside the cursor page â€” all
four apply the cap to rows the query has ALREADY filtered, which is the correct order and also the
cheaper one, because the filter uses an index. `Knowledge` was the only place the order was inverted,
and it was inverted for a reason worth naming: **its filter lived in C# rather than in the query.**

That gives the class a signature you can recognise without reading every projection: **a bounded read
whose `.Where(...)` is applied to the RESULT of the read rather than expressed in it.** If the filter
is in the query the cap cannot be wrong; if it is in the caller, the cap chose the rows before anyone
asked what was wanted. Recorded on DC-035 along with the one residual â€” `Knowledge` still reads each
node's touching assertions at 500 and splits them afterwards, so a document with ~495+ real links
would get an arbitrary 500 with no omission count. No repository measured comes close.

BioHacker 4,420 / 48, meridian 12,613 / 56 â€” every response still inside the frame.

on every branch, that the next push to their branch will run all nine gates, and â€” because it will be
noisy the first time â€” names the two that will fire and how to satisfy them, with a worked example of
the accepted and rejected `Status:` forms. Neither is a new rule; both were always enforced, just not
anywhere they could see them.

**`review-by` on code: decided no, on the user's own rule.** The symmetry is tempting â€” 460 review
dates on documents, so why not flag a stale class? Because nothing in a C# file, a Bicep template or
a SQL script DECLARES when it should next be read. A date could only be manufactured from
last-modified time or churn, and it would render identically to the dates documents actually declare.
A reader could not tell the two apart, which is exactly the failure the no-inference note exists to
prevent. A code artifact gets a review date the moment something writes one down; until then the
absence is accurate.

summary: Upgrade and rollback: journal, snapshot, health gate, coordinator, side-by-side installs, and startup recovery wired into the daemon so the mechanism is used rather than merely present. Ordering is the design — snapshot, journal, migrate, gate, commit — with the point of no return last, because an upgrade that fails halfway leaves a store no binary can read. The 60s gate budget is ENFORCED, keeping the slow replay check asynchronous (P1-PERF: 50k-edge replay vs a 15-minute RTO); a gate that only documented its budget would pass it. THREE DEFECTS FOUND: rollback derived the store path from the snapshot's filename and passed only because the fixture put both in one folder; the atomic replace was not atomic because File.ReadAllText does not share delete, so a concurrent reader made the WRITER throw on Windows; and even after that fix a delete-pending file needs a bounded retry. TWO TESTS PROVED NOTHING until mutation said so — the enum-naming test asserted a round-tripped value, which numeric enums also satisfy, and nothing distinguished atomic replacement from an in-place write. Pruning protects the current build explicitly because after a rollback the current version is an older one. 13/13 mutations caught. 454 tests (+36), four gates clean. Health gate CONTENTS for a real schema migration are not built — the store has no migration chain yet — stated rather than faked.

summary: The first WRITE crosses the boundary: scope refresh. Started-and-polled rather than awaited on the wire, because a scope has a 60s budget and the lane serves one request at a time per connection — the control lane carries commands, and a command that starts long work returns once it is started. The command id is the idempotency key and this is where it first matters across processes; deduplication has two guards and only the concurrent one (TryAdd) is load-bearing, which a mutation run proved by disabling it with nothing failing. Job records are bounded because they are keyed by a caller-chosen id; a running job is never evicted. An incomplete extraction is a failure, not a refresh of zero. Reads and writes are separate seams. summary:
Reported: "the agent sessions do not have my profile or my environment variables — ghcp and claude
are both installed so they should both work."

The verified cause is not in this product. The machine's PATH is 22,297 characters and cmd.exe
silently drops a variable that large, so every .cmd shim — which is every npm-installed CLI — starts
with an EMPTY PATH and cannot find node, git or itself. claude works because claude.exe is a real
executable with no cmd in the path; ghcp does not exist at all, and the Copilot CLI has an npm .cmd
shim. That asymmetry is the entire symptom.

Necessary and sufficient, both measured: at 22,297 characters a cmd child receives an empty PATH,
reproduced twice including once with no part of AI-DE involved; trimmed to 1,799 characters the same
child receives the full PATH. AI-DE passes the environment correctly — PowerShell started from the
same inherited block reads all 22,297 characters and resolves claude.

Five hypotheses were ruled out with evidence, including one flag removed and re-measured, and the
belief that the profile was at fault — which is where two turns of work went first, because the
symptom is indistinguishable from a launcher bug.

The cause of the 22,297 characters: roughly 190 entries of the shape Temp\biohacker-nuget-<guid>\
dotnet-home\.dotnet\tools, appended to the PERSISTED user PATH by another project's build tooling and
never removed. Each is unique, so there is nothing to de-duplicate.

What was ours is the silence. The terminal opened, looked healthy, and the tools were absent with
nothing saying why. EnvironmentHealth.Inspect now states the size, the limit and the largest repeated
group — because 200 unique paths is a number, not a lead — announced once per shell, never per pane.
It does not edit PATH: a tool that silently rewrites the environment to make itself work has hidden
the problem from the only person who can fix it.

Agents are now hosted in the login shell rather than launched beside it, which delivers the profile
half of the request and makes .ps1 shims resolve. It is recorded honestly as NOT fixing the reported
symptom — a .cmd shim invoked from the hosting shell still starts cmd, which still drops the PATH.
Measured, not assumed.

Registered as DC-027: the environment a parent hands a child is not the one the child receives.

summary:
A second language, and a paging defect the second language exposed.

PythonExtractor reads modules, top-level classes and functions, and import edges. Six repositories
had disclosed unread Python before it existed; the disclosure was right and it is not a substitute,
because a graph that says "there is Python here and I cannot see it" is honest and still blind.

It reads STRUCTURE, not semantics, and says so on every scope: imports are not resolved, nested
declarations are invisible, dynamic imports are not followed. Declarations are recognised at column
zero only — an indented def is a method, and claiming it as a module-level function would put a
symbol in the graph that no importer can reach. Import edges are INFERRED, because the target is the
module path as written and whether it resolves to anything is not established here; calling that
Verified is precisely the defect DC-022 is about. A simplify: marker records the ceiling and the
upgrade trigger.

Python also came OFF the unanalysed-languages list on the same day, because a closed gap reported as
open is the same defect as an open one hidden.

Measured on the repository that started this: ai-forward produced ZERO assertions and an empty
disclosure list three turns ago. It now produces 2,158 assertions across 5 scopes in 0.2 seconds,
with its remaining gaps named.

And that run exposed a real paging defect: 2,158 in the store, 2,157 through the paged read.
(subject, predicate, object) is NOT unique — two scopes can assert the same triple — so a cursor over
that ordering silently loses exactly the rows that tie, when a page boundary lands on one. Scope is
part of the ordering and the cursor now, and a test builds two identical Python packages to
manufacture the tie deliberately.

The I/O question was measured rather than assumed and is only half answered. Raw reads of 120 files
cost 5ms outside this product and 73ms on first touch from a different process — a 15x first-access
penalty consistent with on-access scanning. Inside the extractor the same volume costs ~500ms, which
is seven times worse again and is NOT explained. Recorded as a gap rather than a claim; the tree
cache removes the cost on re-index whichever explanation turns out to be right.

summary:
The extraction profile is explained, and both earlier conclusions were artefacts of the benchmark.

A fresh .NET process reading 120 newly-created files took 493ms (4.11ms/file); a SECOND fresh process
over the same files took 6ms, and the repository's own source reads at 0.19ms/file. So the ~500ms
was a one-time, system-wide, per-file cost on the first read after creation — the signature of
on-access scanning — and it never recurs. It is not extraction's cost at all.

Run against a real repository the profile inverts completely. TheTerrace, 463 files in its main
scope: read 53ms, parse 694ms, walk 1,167ms. The walk is the LARGEST cost on real code and looked
free on the synthetic workload, because the generated types were trivial — no inheritance, no
generics, four fields each.

Two independent flaws in one generator, each inverting a published conclusion. Registered as DC-028:
a synthetic benchmark measures the benchmark unless its workload resembles the real one in the
dimensions that drive cost. The control is that the spike prints the same timings for named real
repositories, so the synthetic figure and the real one appear side by side.

Python imports are resolved within their scope now. An import naming a module the scope contains
points at a file that exists and was read, so the edge is VERIFIED; anything else stays INFERRED with
the name as written, because it may be a package, a module in another scope, or nothing, and
asserting which is the guess DC-022 is about. Relative imports resolve against the importing module's
package, one level per leading dot, and climbing above the root resolves to nothing rather than
throwing. On the real Python repository 82 of 330 imports now resolve, and the disclosure carries the
count of those that do not — a blanket "imports are not resolved" became a closed gap reported as
open the moment resolution landed.

The cursor audit found one more thing and cleared another. ResultBounds.NextCursor is ALWAYS null and
no projection returning it pages — said out loud in the type, because a caller could loop on it and
never leave the first page with nothing failing. And DeriveClaimCurrent folds statuses with Max under
a comment saying the weakest wins: correct only because the enum is ordered strongest-first, so a
reordering would silently invert it into manufacturing confidence. Pinned by a test.

summary:
The graph surface had never shown a graph.

Reported by the user, comparing TheTerrace in this tool against the same repository in Obsidian: two
nodes versus a full graph. The cause was not extraction — the store held 12,100 assertions across
2,164 nodes — it was that the canvas called FindAsync with a limit of ONE to pick a root and then
drew that root's neighbours. A workspace of two thousand nodes rendered as the alphabetically first
symbol and its single neighbour, correctly, from the day it was written. Four unit tests described
that behaviour approvingly.

GraphProjection answers the question the surface exists for: every node and edge, bounded by a cap
that is reported rather than silent. Attributes fold onto nodes instead of being drawn as edges — a
has_type arrow would put the string "class" in the graph as a thing other things point at — using the
same single definition the search already applies. LoadAsync with no root now means the whole graph;
a root means drill-down. Proven across the daemon as well, because every cross-boundary defect so far
has been right in process and wrong through the pipe.

A second finding sat inside the first. With the graph finally visible, its six most-connected nodes
were string, int, Task<TResult>, DateTimeOffset, IReadOnlyList<T> and Guid — 773 edges to string
alone. A graph whose centre is the BCL is not a picture of anybody's domain, and a cap ordered by raw
degree drops the user's own types to keep framework primitives. Nodes carry IsExternal now (nothing
in the workspace declares them) and declared nodes are kept first. The same repository's centre
became AppDbContext, Fixture, SportMonksProvider, ScheduledRefresh.

Registered as DC-031: a surface asks a narrower question than the one it exists to answer. The
generalisation is one question — what is the cardinality of what this shows, against the cardinality
of what it fetched — and the related tell is a test suite that describes the slice fluently.

TheTerrace now: 28 scopes, 13,530 assertions, 2,813 nodes and 8,602 edges with nothing omitted.
TypeScript is read, and the symbol walk is profiled.

TypeScriptExtractor closes the largest remaining disclosure — typescript-not-analysed (165 files) on
a repository whose C# half was fully mapped. Same bargain as Python: structure, not semantics.
Exported top-level class, interface, type, enum, function and const; import and re-export
specifiers; nothing inside a function or a namespace block. Declaration files (.d.ts) are skipped
because they re-state types defined elsewhere and indexing them would put every symbol in the graph
twice, once with nothing behind it.

Specifiers resolve only when RELATIVE and only to a file this scope contains — extensions optional,
a directory meaning its index file. A bare specifier is a package or a path alias and resolving it
needs configuration this extractor deliberately does not read, so it stays Inferred with the
specifier as written. TypeScript and JavaScript left the unanalysed-languages list the same day.

It is deliberately NOT a shared base with PythonExtractor. They look alike and are not the same:
TypeScript's specifiers carry extensions and index files, its declarations are export-gated rather
than column-zero, and JSX changes what a valid line looks like. A base parameterised by all of that
is more machinery than either extractor contains; a third language that fits the pattern is when the
abstraction is earned.

Indexing TheTerrace with it immediately raised a real store error: two files can share a module name
— app.ts beside a compiled app.js — so the same triple was asserted twice in one scope and the
natural key rejected it, correctly. Identical facts are one fact, so both extractors deduplicate
before returning. Silencing the key would have weakened a control that is doing its job.

And the symbol walk, which the real-repository profile named as the largest cost, is now split:
enumerating the namespace tree is 135ms for 1,026 types, and reading each type's members is 1,074ms
— about 89% of the walk and half the whole scope. The next hypothesis worth testing is
ToDisplayString, called per symbol, but that is a hypothesis and is written down as one rather than
acted on.

summary:
The hypothesis that `ToDisplayString` dominated the symbol walk was **wrong**, and measuring it found
a much larger defect than the one it was looking for.

Splitting the walk by operation: display 46ms across 7,312 calls — **3.9%**. The real costs were
depends-on 613ms (51%) and attributes 403ms (34%). The attribute cost was one call:
`FluentTableMappings` ran `DescendantNodes()` over all 1,026 type declarations, hunting an EF
`ToTable` call. Hoisting it to the compilation with a source-text prefilter cut it to 1ms of
prefilter across 465 files and 217ms of walking the 66 that survived.

Then the 66 files were the finding. Most were EF migration `*.Designer.cs` snapshots — and the three
that were not revealed that the reader **did not work**. It matched `Entity<T>()...ToTable("x")` as a
single expression. TheTerrace, like most EF codebases, writes:

    var terrace = modelBuilder.Entity<Terrace>();
    terrace.ToTable("Terrace", "setup");

So the extractor recovered **1 declared mapping and guessed 123**, on a repository that states every
one of them outright. Every one of those 123 inferred `maps_to` edges was a name-matching guess
standing where a declaration already existed. The same reader also emitted the entity name as
written in source (`Order`) where every other assertion uses the display string (`Shop.Order`) — so
even its successes were edges whose subject matched no node.

Resolved semantically now: ask the model for the RECEIVER's type. One rule answers every style —
chained, local-variable, lambda-configuration, `IEntityTypeConfiguration<T>` — because in all of them
the receiver is an `EntityTypeBuilder<TEntity>`, and the symbol's display string is the name the rest
of the extractor emits. **Verified joins 1 → 64, inferred 123 → 73, `declares_table` facts 63.**

Generated files are skipped, on correctness grounds before performance ones: EF writes a model
snapshot per migration, each calling `ToTable` for every entity *as it stood then*, so reading them
asserts a table renamed three migrations ago as current fact wearing the same Verified badge. 63 of
the 66 files were these. `fluent-scan` fell 1,418ms → 60ms warm as a side effect, not as the goal.
The skip is disclosed with a count, because skipped is not absent.

DC-032 registered: **a reader recognises one spelling of a pattern and reports the rest as absent.**
The signature is a ratio nobody looks at — precise hits against fallback hits on real input — and it
survives because the fallback is doing its job, so the surface looks populated and coverage stays
green. The control was observed failing with the skip disabled.

**Module ids were colliding, certainly rather than theoretically.** Both module-shaped extractors
named a module by its path relative to its OWN SCOPE, and a scope is one directory. Every Python
package has an `__init__.py`, so a repository with five packages produced five scopes each declaring
a module called `__init__` — one node in the graph carrying the merged edges of five unrelated files.
The same for `index.ts`, `main`, `setup`, `conftest`. Ids are now the repository-relative path:
unique by construction, readable, and the string a person would type to open the file.

That made cross-scope resolution possible, which was the actual next step. An import naming a sibling
package resolves to a file in a different scope, so it could never resolve from inside the one doing
the importing. `ExtractionRequest` now carries the workspace's module set, computed once per revision
from the FILESYSTEM — not from the store, because resolving against what has already been extracted
would make an edge depend on the order the scopes happened to run in, the trap the Python extractor
already avoids one level down. Null means "not supplied", which is not "there is nothing there": the
edge stays Inferred and the disclosure fires.

A test comment had encoded the defective rule approvingly — *"modules are named relative to it:
`models`, not `src/models`"* — which is DC-031's tell in its own words.

**The graph surface is now queryable, not just fetchable.** `GraphQuery` filters by kind, by scope,
and by whether to include nodes nothing declares. The filter runs BEFORE the cap and degree is
counted over what survives it: filtering afterwards would rank and trim the whole graph and only then
discard, so a caller asking for the domain model would receive the wrong 5,000 nodes trimmed to the
right kind, with nothing in the result saying so. Proven across the daemon as well as in process,
because every cross-boundary defect here so far has been right in process and wrong through the pipe.

**A next step I listed last turn was wrong and is withdrawn.** "The index still walks every scope" —
it does not. `ScopeFingerprints` already skips an unchanged scope and counts it as *reused* rather
than *indexed*, deliberately, so "28 of 28 indexed" cannot be a true sentence about a run that read
nothing. I asserted its absence without opening the file. The residual — incrementality BELOW the
scope, so a one-file edit does not re-walk 1,026 types — is real, but it conflicts with the
append-only per-scope snapshot model and is a design decision, not a tidy-up.

summary:
Two more performance hypotheses died, and the second death is the useful one.

Splitting `depends_on`: **`SymbolEqualityComparer` dedupe is 3ms of 600ms — 0.5%** across 13,906 raw
symbols. Gather is 597ms. So the cost of `depends_on` IS the semantic work — `GetMembers()` binding
every member signature — and it cannot be made cheaper, only avoided. Two turns, two suspects
(`ToDisplayString` at 3.9%, then the comparer at 0.5%), both wrong, both named before being believed.
The measurement is now fine-grained enough that the next guess has nowhere to hide.

**Generated types are excluded from the whole extractor**, not just the fluent scan — a type is
dropped only when EVERY file declaring it is auto-generated, so a partial class with a hand-written
half (a WPF window, an EF migration people edit) is kept. Disclosed with a count.

**And the estimate that motivated it was wrong.** I predicted ~600 excluded types on TheTerrace. The
real number is **1**. EF marks only the snapshot half (`*.Designer.cs`) as generated; the migration
half starts with a plain `using System;`, so each migration type has a hand-written declaration and
is correctly kept. The rule is right and its effect here is small — recorded that way rather than
quietly dropped, because "I expected 600 and got 1" is the part worth knowing.

**Routes are answerable now.** `GraphPaths` returns how one node reaches another: shortest routes
only, directed (walking an edge backwards would answer "these are related" while looking like "a
change here reaches there"), with the route's status taken from its WEAKEST edge so one inferred link
cannot launder itself into a verified chain. A missing endpoint returns a reason, not an empty list
that reads as "unconnected". Proven across the daemon pipe as well as in process — a path is the one
result shaped as a list of lists, so it is the one most likely to arrive flattened.

**The id-allocator gap is closed, and closing it found two more allocators.**
`tools/verify-id-allocators.py` asks the generalising question behind DC-013 — *what else here is
numbered by reading the highest and adding one?* — as a check rather than a note. It guards five
families in one place (adding one is a line, not a script) and reports any UNDECLARED sequence, so
the next allocator is guarded on the day it is invented. Observed failing on both shapes before it
was believed.

On its first run it found `adr-` (16 decisions, allocated by FILENAME — a kind the first draft could
not even express) and, on inspection, `INV-`, which was below the threshold at two entries and was
declared anyway.

Two first-draft errors are recorded in DC-013 because they are the interesting part. It reported
eighteen holes in the audit log as failures — but a hole is the merge protocol working: a contested
id is resolved by re-issuing the loser, leaving the number unused. Verified with `git log -S`: none
of the missing ids has ever existed, so nothing was lost. **A control that flags the fix as the
defect is how a control teaches people to ignore it**, so contiguity is opt-in per family now. It
also first read ADR ids out of `architecture.md`, which only cites them — an allocator is where an id
is CREATED, never where it is mentioned.

**Electing a single allocator between sessions was considered and rejected** (the user asked). The
sessions work in separate worktrees on purpose and an election needs a rendezvous they do not have:
a session an hour into its work has not fetched, so "ask the allocator" is stale or a blocking round
trip through `main`, and it would make one session wait on another to record a lesson. The class is
not "the wrong allocator won", it is "a shared sequence with two writers".

**Sub-scope incrementality is written up, not built.** `docs/notes/note-20260830-sub-scope-
incrementality.md` states four options with what each costs, recommends one (keep the atomic
generation, skip the walk for unchanged types) and explicitly does not take it: the per-scope and
per-parse layers already exist, and nobody has measured whether edit-to-graph latency is a 1.2s
on-demand cost or a per-keystroke one. Instrumenting that is cheaper than any of the four options and
should come first. The decision changes the store's contract, so it is the user's call.

A build gap worth naming: the spike project is not in `AiDe.sln`, so last turn's solution build never
compiled it and the first measurement this turn silently ran a **stale binary**. Caught because the
new timing fields did not appear in the output.

summary:
**The measurement the sub-scope decision was blocked on now exists.** A refresh had a span but its
STATUS carried no duration, so the only thing a caller could read was how many assertions came back.
`ScopeRefreshStatus` now carries `QueuedMilliseconds` and `DurationMilliseconds` — kept separate
because waiting is a concurrency problem and running is a cost problem, and one number hides which
one a user is feeling. `RefreshMetrics` adds p50/p95/max over a bounded window plus first/last
observed, exposed over IPC as `refresh.metrics` with no request body and no failure mode: an operator
asking what re-indexing costs should never be told it depends on what they enable first.

summary:
The graph was found by a user opening a repository, not by us, so every other read operation was
measured at its own ceiling against the 1 MiB frame. **Two more were one repository away from
INV-0003, and a third could never have succeeded.**

| operation | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| evidence (2,000/page) | 1,004,397 B — **95.8% of the frame** | 659,164 B, 1,310 rows, cursor continues |
| graph (5,000-node ceiling) | 1,522,915 B — **overflows** | 474,437 B, shrunk to fit, `Omitted` reports |
| find (20,000 ceiling) | 461,750 B returned while **reporting a 64 KiB cap** | byte-bounded, `ByteCapped` set |

The class behind all three: **every ceiling in the read surface counts ITEMS and the transport limit
is in BYTES**, and every item's size comes from repository content. A count-only cap admits an
unbounded payload. `Evidence`'s own documentation claimed a page "can cross a pipe without breaching
the result-byte cap" — it was fifteen times over that cap. `Find` declared `MaxBytes: 65,536` beside
461,750 bytes of results, a control that could not fire (DC-016).

Truncating an evidence page is **lossless**, which is why the bound belongs in the projection: the
cursor continues from the last row actually returned, so it costs a round trip and never a row. A
test pages a corpus to exhaustion and asserts every assertion comes back exactly once. Every response
keeps at least one item — a caller that receives nothing because its first row is enormous can never
make progress.

The byte guard uses a **measured** constant, not a guessed one: 2,000 assertions whose fields total
238,002 bytes serialise to 1,004,397, so JSON scaffolding is **383 bytes per row**. Rounded up,
because a guard that under-counts is a guard that lets the frame overflow.

**The sub-scope-incrementality decision is resolved, and not by the instrument built for it.** The
note said the answer depended on how often edit-to-graph happens, and `RefreshMetrics` was built to
measure that. One grep answered it instead: **there is no `FileSystemWatcher` anywhere in `src/`**.
Indexing runs only from explicit commands, so the cost is paid deliberately by a user pressing a
button. Breaking the per-scope snapshot's atomicity to shorten a deliberate 1.2s action is a poor
trade, so none of options A–D is built. The note stays, status `resolved`, naming the trigger that
would change it: **re-index on save**, which converts a bounded cost into a per-edit one.

Worth recording because it nearly went the other way. Three hypotheses in this area have now been
wrong — `ToDisplayString` (3.9%), `SymbolEqualityComparer` (0.5%), "the index still walks every
scope" (it does not). This would have been the fourth: collecting a distribution and reasoning
carefully about a number that answered a question nobody was asking.

**My own new gate cried wolf and is fixed.** `verify-id-allocators` reported an undeclared family
called `nDC-` — it was matching the `n` of a JSON-escaped newline before a *mentioned* `DC-` id in a
log summary. A mention is not an allocation, which is the same distinction the first draft got wrong

excluded from the candidate scan: a record of a mention must never nominate an allocator. This is the
second time this script has flagged correct behaviour as a defect; a control that does that twice is
one people switch off.

**SQL scripts are folded, not just read.** MEASURED: one repository carries **125 `ALTER TABLE … ADD`**
statements, so reading `CREATE` alone showed its schema as it stood at the first migration and called
that current. Adds, `DROP COLUMN` and `DROP TABLE` are now applied in file order — drops especially,
because a column that no longer exists is a **wrong** fact rather than a missing one. Renames are
counted and disclosed rather than guessed: every dialect spells them differently, and guessing
produces a confidently wrong column name.

**Three gates I wrote this session were not in CI.** `verify-id-allocators`,
`verify-project-coverage` and `verify-bounds-are-enforced` sat in `tools/` for several commits with
no workflow line — they ran only when I remembered. A gate nobody invokes is the "lesson recorded as
prose" failure wearing an executable's clothes: it looks like a control in every review and fires
never. All three wired, and `verify-project-coverage` now asks the same question about gates that it
asks about projects — **what exists to be run, and is not run.** Observed failing with a gate removed
from the workflow.

**The `simplify:` marker audit found one triggered and one premise already false.** `IpcFraming`'s
trigger fired during INV-0003 — and the answer was **none of the two exits the marker listed**.
Neither a bigger frame nor a data lane: the operation did not legitimately need to carry more. A
2,815-node hairball was never a useful answer and the spec had always said so, so every response was
bounded below the cap instead. Recorded, because a marker naming two exits invites you to take one.

Its stated premise — *"a control lane carries envelopes, not payloads: the largest legitimate message
is a command with a small JSON body"* — was **already false when audited**: ordinary responses are an
evidence page at 659,164 bytes, a graph at 475,223, an overview at 345,507. That sentence had not
been re-read since it was true. The other twelve markers were reviewed with no evidence of firing.

**"Verified joins for non-EF repositories" turned out to be the wrong question, and the finding is
better than the feature.** BioHacker has zero `DbContext` files, zero `[Table]` attributes and 191
SQL literals naming tables from inside store classes. There is **no declaration of a code→schema
mapping to verify** — and there should not be one invented. A store class issuing four statements
against three tables is not *mapped* to any of them.

What the source does declare is **usage**, so that is what is emitted: `uses_table`, Verified because
the literal is in the type. **62 edges on BioHacker**, structure it simply did not have. Deliberately
not `maps_to` — reusing the mapping predicate would launder usage into a mapping exactly where a
reader trusts it (DC-022's shape). Joins there remain 0 verified / 8 inferred, which is the honest
answer.

**Deduplication moved into one place on its third copy.** Python and TypeScript each grew the same
six lines after the same raw `UNIQUE constraint failed` from mid-index; `uses_table` hit it a third
time immediately, because one store names the same table in four statements. `ExtractionFacts.Distinct`
now owns it, so the fourth extractor inherits it. The store's key stays strict — silencing it would
trade a loud correct failure for a quiet wrong graph.

**And "make the measurement a CI nightly" was wrong, stated rather than quietly dropped.** The

summary:
**I shipped a defect last turn and this turn's sweep caught it.** The `uses_table` reader matched a
SQL keyword followed by a word ANYWHERE in a string literal, so *"we update the record"* produced an
edge to a table called `the`. MEASURED: 63 prose strings in TheTerrace, and its `uses_table` count
fell from **150 to 56** once the reader required a statement SHAPE.

Under-matching hides real facts; over-matching invents them — and the invented ones are worse,
because they arrive labelled **Verified**. Same root cause as DC-033 in the opposite direction: the
matcher's fit to real input had never been measured. **A matcher is not finished until you know both
what it misses and what it invents.**

**The naive fix broke the real case, which is exactly why both directions must be measured
together.** Requiring each literal to begin with a verb found **nothing at all** on the repository
that motivated the feature — real code splits SQL across concatenated literals, and the fragment
holding `FROM dbo.AssessmentJob` begins with `FROM`. The reader folds the `+` chain and reads it as
one statement; a chain containing anything non-literal is skipped whole rather than half-read.

A smaller lesson: the regex form of that shape test silently returned false for
`"INSERT INTO dbo.AssessmentJob (…)"` — a string plainly beginning with one of its own alternatives —
and cost more to diagnose than the check was worth. It is explicit code now.

**`uses_table` reaches the Joins pane.** A distinct kind, never folded into `maps_to`: a store class
issuing four statements against three tables is not mapped to any of them, and counting usage as
mapping would make the verified/inferred ratio the pane exists to show meaningless. BioHacker's pane
goes from **0 verified / 8 inferred to 57 / 8** — a repository that showed nothing now shows what its
code actually touches.

**Step 2 needed no work and step 3 was answered by measurement.** The EF reader ALREADY folds
`CreateTable`, `AddColumn`, `DropColumn`, `DropTable`, `RenameTable` and raw `Sql` — I assumed it
might not, without checking, which is the habit this session keeps catching. Measured against real
usage: the operations it does not handle (`CreateIndex` 113, `AddForeignKey` 19, `AlterColumn`) do
not change which tables or columns EXIST. One genuine gap found and closed: `RenameColumn` was
unhandled with no default case, so a renamed column silently kept its old name — a wrong fact. EF
states renames in named arguments, so unlike raw SQL it is simply readable.

**Python and TypeScript do not embed SQL, so nothing was built for them.** The counts looked
promising — 186, 61, 1,162 "SQL literals" — and sampling showed *"update the"*, *"select more than
one option from this"*, and **zero** files containing `insert into`. Building `uses_table` there
would have emitted edges from English prose. Evidence for NOT building something is worth as much as
evidence for building it.

**The measurement log earns its keep at two readings.** Verified joins across the three repositories
moved **64 → 120**, **0 → 57**, **35 → 50**, with assertion counts slightly DOWN as prose noise left
the graph. One reading is a point; two is a direction, and the drift is now in `git diff` rather than
in my memory of last turn's numbers.

summary:
**The invent-direction of DC-033 now has a control, and it found four more defects on its first
run.** `ExtractorsDoNotInventTests` feeds every reader a corpus with no declarations and plenty of
text SHAPED like declarations, and asserts it produces nothing but disclosures:

- the **SQL** reader read `-- CREATE TABLE Ghost` and `/* CREATE TABLE Historical */` as tables;
- the **TypeScript** reader read `export class Removed {}` out of a block comment;
- the **Python** reader read a class out of a **docstring** — the one place its column-zero rule
  cannot tell documentation from declaration;
- the **C#** reader turned *"delete from your account to remove it"* into `table:your`, because that
  sentence genuinely begins with a SQL verb and last turn's shape test could not reject it.

**Commented-out code is the worst possible input for a line-oriented reader**, and every repository
is full of it — it is real syntax, because it *was* code. `SourceText` blanks comments before any
reader believes a line, keeping newlines so provenance line numbers stay true. The C# case needed a
second rule: a real table reference **ends where a clause can begin** — a keyword, punctuation, or
the end of the statement. In prose the next token is just another word.

**Two things the fixes got wrong first, kept because they are the lesson.** Blanking string contents
for SQL deleted `"main"."Thing"`: in SQL a double quote is a quoted IDENTIFIER, not a string, so the
reader lost the very names it exists to find — caught by a test in seconds, which is the cheapest
possible way to learn that two languages disagree about a quote character. And `PRINT 'about to
create table X'` names no table while `EXEC('CREATE TABLE …')` does; the reader can tell neither from
the other, so it reads neither and discloses the count.

**Step 1 was answered by measurement and needed no change.** The Bicep and context readers were swept
on a repository they were not written against: Bicep's matchers are line-anchored on `resource`,
`module` and `param`, and their values came back as real parameter names (`sqlServerName`,
`identityName`) and real Azure types — nothing invented. The context map's `*` is a documented suffix
wildcard and the real patterns end at a `.` boundary. Both pinned by the new control so they stay
that way.

**The third reading shows the CORRECTION, which is what a third reading is for.** Verified joins:

    TheTerrace                64 -> 120 -> 95
    BioHacker                  0 ->  57 -> 55
    meridian-finance-planner  35 ->  50 -> 46

The middle number was inflated by prose; the last is the honest one. **A single reading would have
recorded 120 as progress**, and two readings would have recorded it as a trend.

**On `AlterColumn` — the decision, not an assumption.** It is not folded, and should not be. The
graph's `has_column` records that a column EXISTS; `AlterColumn` changes a type or nullability, which
that fact does not carry, so folding it would change nothing observable. Recording types is a
different feature — it would need a fact shape that can express them, both schema readers agreeing on
it, and a consumer that wants it. None of those exists, so this stays where it is: named in the
extractor's `simplify:` ceiling as the upgrade trigger, rather than half-built.

summary:
**The knowledge graph was never being populated, and the reason is worse than a bug.** The reader had
existed since Phase 1, with tests, inside the fixture extractor. `CompositeExtractor` had a route for
it. And `CSharpScopeDiscovery` produced six scope kinds — `csharp`, `bicep`, `schema`, `python`,
`typescript`, `sql` — and **no knowledge scope at all**. The capability was correct, tested, and
unreachable on every real repository for the life of the project.

Both halves passed their own tests. The producer is proven by unit tests that hand it input; the
router is proven by fixtures that name the scope explicitly. Only DISCOVERY was untested against
reality, and its gap is invisible from either side.

**A zero that means "nobody looked" reads as "there is none"** — which is the shape this product
exists to avoid, in the product's own headline surface, on a repository whose premise is that *docs
hold intent, code holds reality, and the expensive defects live in the gap*. Half of that sentence
was never being read.

MEASURED after wiring discovery, on this repository: **466 `owned_by`, 346 `refines`, 287
`implements`, 272 `relates-to`, 66 `depends-on`**, centred on `knowledge-hub` with 78 edges. Scopes
across the three measured repositories: **28→66, 34→48, 34→56**. Every response still fits the frame.

**Running it over real documents immediately found two defects in the new reader** — which is the
lesson from last turn applied one turn later:

- link lines carry a trailing YAML comment, and trimming from the END left it attached: the graph
  gained a relation literally called `implements }   # typed edges — registry in …`. Parsing now
  stops at the closing brace.
- **templates** carry frontmatter in exactly the shape a real document does, with `<artifact-id>`
  where the id goes — so they became nodes describing the shape of a document, linked to things that
  do not exist. Excluded by filename and, independently, by rejecting angle-bracketed placeholders.

DC-041 registered: **a capability is complete, tested, and nothing ever routes work to it.** The
signature is a count that is exactly zero on every real repository while a sibling count is large,
and the question that finds it is *"what produces the keys this router matches on, and does it
produce this one?"*. The control compares the two lists in a test instead of in somebody's head:
`EveryRouteHasAProducerAndEveryProducerHasARoute` fails if discovery emits a kind nothing routes, or
if a route exists that nothing discovers.

**The other next steps, carried:**

- **Bicep is comment-stripped too.** It PASSED the invent control — line-anchored matchers, and a
  sweep of an unfamiliar repository produced only real parameter names and real Azure types. Stripped

- **Provenance line numbers are asserted, not assumed.** Comments are blanked rather than deleted

  declared after a multi-line comment. It was the reason for the design and had never been checked.
- **The invent control now runs against real repository text**, which is how both knowledge defects

- **`GraphQuery` filters: ANSWERED by the user — presets, three named views.** Recorded in the

summary:
**INV-0004's root cause was a Phase-1 assumption that six extractors later made false.** Node
classification read:

    var isKnowledge = result.Assertions.Any(a => a.Subject == nodeId && a.Predicate == "has_type");

*Anything with a type is knowledge* — true when the fixture reader was the only producer of
`has_type`, and false the moment a second extractor emitted it. By now every C# class, table, bicep
resource and python module carried one, so almost the entire graph was classified `knowledge`, and it
surfaced exactly as the design session saw it: a bicep resource reading **"kind: knowledge"**. DC-022
precisely — a predicate gained producers and a consumer kept its assumption about who emits it.

**Fixed by having the PRODUCER declare it.** Scope-id prefixes were the first attempt and were nearly
right, but the fixture reader emits knowledge from a scope not named for it, so the id could not be
the authority either. A fact can be: both knowledge-reading paths now emit `node_class = knowledge`,
and the core classifies from that. Nothing infers a node's half of the graph from a type name again.

**Neighbours carry their real kind.** `DescribeResult` gained `NeighborKinds`; the canvas hardcoded
`"source"` for every neighbour because the projection did not carry one, so a drill-down showed a
table, a bicep resource and a class as the same thing and the filter could not tell them apart. A
renderer inventing a default is a renderer stating a fact it does not have.

**`UpsertNode` is a no-op when nothing changed.** It is a Type-2 dimension and every call closed the
current row and opened a new one, so re-indexing rewrote the history of every unchanged node. History
whose every row is an artefact of re-running the indexer cannot answer the question it exists for.

**The knowledge pane was returning code.** It filtered on `has_type` alone — the same stale
assumption, one projection along — so now that knowledge is finally indexed it would have shown C#
classes beside ADRs. It filters on `node_class` now, which is the dimension that knows.

**`review-by` is read and overdue reviews are a health finding.** 460 review dates on this repository.
`owned_by` and `review_by` joined the attribute set: a person and a date are not things to navigate
to, and drawing them would have put "@someone" and "2027-02-28" in the graph as peers of the
documents that carry them.

**The one "document with no id" was a false positive of mine.** `INSTALL.md` opens with `doc:`,
`bundle_version:` and `changes:` — a pack manifest that happens to use YAML, never a graph node. The
complaint now fires only when the frontmatter is GRAPH frontmatter (a type, owner, links or review
date) and still has no id. Same mistake as reading prose into a schema, one field along.

**The code↔knowledge join is NOT buildable today, and that is the finding.** Measured: **no knowledge
link in this repository targets a code symbol** — every `to:` names another document id. There is no
declared relationship to read, and inferring one from titles or namespaces is exactly the guessing
this codebase refuses. What would unblock it is a change to how docs are WRITTEN, not to the reader:
a link such as `- { to: TheTerrace.Features.Fixtures, rel: governs }`. Recorded rather than invented.

vocabulary.

summary:
**The Knowledge chip read 0 on a repository holding 2,343 knowledge nodes. Two causes, both Core's.**

**The store was cached from a build that had no knowledge reader.** `ScopeFingerprints` already
carried an `ExtractorGeneration` for exactly this — a constant in every fingerprint so that upgrading
the product invalidates the sidecar — and nobody bumped it. So the knowledge extractor, `node_class`,
comment stripping in four readers, the SQL fold and `uses_table` all shipped while every existing
workspace kept serving results produced by the previous generation. Bumped to `2026-08-30.1`; an
upgraded app now rebuilds rather than reusing.

**And the graph carried only each node's FINE kind.** MEASURED: TheTerrace's knowledge types are
`spec` and **`knowledge-epl-fan-platform`** — a name that repository invented. A chip matching a
fixed list of type names cannot work across repositories, and widening the list only moves the
problem to the next one (DC-033). `GraphNode.IsKnowledge` carries the DECLARED coarse dimension, so a
filter asks the question instead of recognising spellings.

Verified end to end: TheTerrace now yields **2,343 `node_class`, 639 `owned_by`, 428 `refines`, 114
`spec`** — 24,058 assertions across 66 scopes, every response still inside the frame.

**The code↔knowledge join is closed by decision, not deferred.** The user's rule: *"It's ok if docs
and code are not linkable and orthogonal, they will tend to be orthogonal which is why pruning the
graph on one or the other is a meaningful cut. Do not infer — the graph should only be on observable
links/relationships."*

Recorded as a decision note, because it is a standing principle rather than one answer: **an edge is
a claim that something in the repository says so.** Orthogonality is information — because the two
halves are separate, "show the knowledge" and "show the code" are exact cuts rather than blurred
ones. Inference would have made membership depend on how good the guess was that day, and this
codebase has paid for that twice already (`depends_on` produced 7,426 false Verified edges;
`uses_table` turned *"we update the record"* into a table called `the`). What would legitimately
unblock a join is a link written down — `- { to: TheTerrace.Features.Fixtures, rel: governs }` — which
the frontmatter reader would index today with no code change.

**Python dynamic and nested declarations: measured, and NOT built.** Dynamic imports are unobservable
statically, so reading them would be inference — ruled out by the principle above. Nested
declarations are observable but MEASURED at 28/31/21 against 356/457/150 top-level across three
repositories (~7%), and they are implementation details inside functions with no type information to
build edges from: the graph would gain volume, not structure. The existing disclosures already state
exactly this. INV-0004's fourth handoff closes as a priority call answered.

costs the reader the time the control saved.**
